# oprobe — full documentation

> Every page of the oprobe documentation in one file (generated from README.md and docs/; see llms.txt for the index).


<!-- source: README.md -->

# oprobe

**See every request your object-storage client makes. Know where the time and the money go, and what to change.**

oprobe drives realistic workloads through [Apache OpenDAL](https://opendal.apache.org/) against S3, GCS,
Azure Blob, R2, OSS, COS, B2, MinIO or local storage and traces **every backend request**: time queued,
DNS/TCP/proxy/TLS on new connections, sending, waiting for the first byte, transferring, and waiting for your
code. It names the cause of what it finds, backs it with evidence, says what to change and how to verify it.
Every run is saved as one `.oprobe` file you can reopen, compare, export or hand to an agent.

It is built for people (a terminal, a native app, a single-file HTML report), for CI (a GitHub Action, exit
codes, Markdown/JUnit) and for agents (JSON everywhere, an event stream, an MCP server).

[中文](README.zh-CN.md) · [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) · [Concepts](docs/concepts.md) ·
[CLI reference](docs/cli.md) · [Reading the report](docs/reading-the-report.md) · [Metrics](docs/metrics.md) ·
[Workloads](docs/workloads.md) · [CI](docs/ci.md) · [Install](docs/install.md) · [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md)

## Start in 60 seconds

```bash
# 1. install (macOS / Linux; Windows and packages: docs/install.md)
curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh

# 2. see what oprobe finds, with no account and no flags
oprobe demo

# 3. your bucket
oprobe target add prod s3://my-bucket/oprobe --region eu-west-1
oprobe run prod
```

`oprobe demo` starts a local S3 lab that throttles above 24 requests in flight and turns 1 in 40 requests into
stragglers, measures it with 32 workers for 8 seconds and explains, step by step, what it found. `oprobe run`
without a target asks what to measure: the demo, the AWS profiles, Google credentials or Azure variables it
finds on your machine, or a URL — and saves your choice as a named target.

```text
$ oprobe run prod
[CRITICAL] Throttling-bound: the service rejected 3.6% of requests with 429/503;
  ✖ 626 throttled responses (429/503)
    3.57% of requests throttled; 609 retries, 63.02s total backoff (25% of operat…
    → The service is rate-limiting this request rate. Lower `concurrency` / `max…
  ▲ `read.full` p99 is 50.9× its median
    p50 5.04ms · p99 257ms · max 663ms
    → See the slowest-operation timelines for the responsible stage. Server stra…
  2114.0 ops/s · 119.2 MiB/s · p50 5.04ms · p99 257ms · errors 0.10%
  626 throttled · SLA met
full report: oprobe runs show 20261120-084637-d873
```

The default output is at most 20 lines that fit 80 columns: the verdict, the top findings (cause · evidence ·
advice · next command), the key numbers, and where the full report is.

## Look closer

| | |
|---|---|
| `oprobe runs show last` | The full report in the terminal (80 columns; `--detail` for everything). |
| `oprobe runs show last -o html > report.html` | One self-contained HTML file: charts with real axes, a latency heatmap, the slowest operations as request waterfalls, every request in a filterable table. Works offline, light and dark, prints cleanly. |
| `oprobe runs open last` | The run in the native app. |
| `oprobe compare base last` | A regression gate between two runs (exit 3 on regression). |
| `oprobe tune prod` | The best client configuration that does not trip throttling, as a profile and Rust/Python code. |
| `oprobe runs list` | Every saved run: when, verdict, ops/s, p99, cost. |

![The HTML report of the demo run](docs/images/report-html.png)

## The app

Run `oprobe` with no arguments: a native window (AppKit on macOS, Win32/Direct2D on Windows, GTK 4 on Linux)
when there is a display, the same workbench in your terminal otherwise (`oprobe top`, also over SSH). Targets,
run history and baselines on the left; the run inspector with Overview, Requests, Timeline, Connections,
Findings and Cost; the selected request or operation on the right. [More →](docs/app.md)

![oprobe workbench](docs/images/app-workbench.png)

## What it answers

| Question | How |
|---|---|
| Network, server or my client? | Each operation's wall time split into queue / connect / upload / server / download / retry / client from the real request timeline. |
| Why is p99 so much worse than p50? | The slowest operations keep every request with its stages, connection (cold/warm), status and request ID, plus an async call stack captured while they were stuck. |
| Is it throttling? | 429/503 counts, Retry-After, retry backoff as its own share of time, and the concurrency where it starts (`oprobe tune`). |
| Are connections reused? Is TLS slow? | Per-dial DNS/TCP/proxy/TLS times, reuse ratio, peak in-flight requests, per remote address. |
| Am I paying for bytes I do not use? | Read amplification, over-read from range coalescing, requests per operation. |
| What will it cost? | The measured request mix × provider price tables, waste from failed requests and over-reads. |
| Did my change make storage I/O worse? | `oprobe compare` or the GitHub Action: noise floors, configuration differences, Markdown + JUnit. |

## In CI

```yaml
- uses: hxddh/oprobe@v3
  with:
    target: s3://ci-bucket/oprobe
    preset: small-files
    baseline: main
```

The action installs a pinned oprobe, runs, compares against the baseline, uploads the `.oprobe` file and the
HTML report, keeps one sticky PR comment up to date and fails on regression. [CI guide →](docs/ci.md)

## For agents

Every command prints one JSON document with `-o json` and an event stream with `-o ndjson`; errors carry stable
codes and exit codes; `oprobe schema` prints the JSON Schemas; `oprobe mcp` is an MCP server (read-only unless
`--allow-write`). See [docs/agents.md](docs/agents.md) and [llms.txt](llms.txt).

## Install

| Platform | |
|---|---|
| macOS / Linux | `curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh \| sh` |
| Windows | `winget install hxddh.oprobe`, the `.msi`, or `irm https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 \| iex` |
| Homebrew | `oprobe.rb` (CLI) and `oprobe.cask.rb` (the app) in every release — [docs/install.md](docs/install.md#homebrew) |
| Debian / Ubuntu, Fedora / RHEL | `.deb` / `.rpm` from the release page |
| Rust | `cargo install oprobe --locked` (`--features gui` for the window on Linux) |

The macOS and Windows packages are **not code-signed** (no certificates): the first open needs one
confirmation — [how](docs/install.md#first-open-of-unsigned-packages). Every asset has a SHA-256 in
`SHA256SUMS` and a signed SLSA build provenance attestation (`gh attestation verify`). Update with
`oprobe self-update` (or your package manager).

oprobe sends no telemetry. It talks only to the storage you point it at, and to GitHub when you run
`oprobe self-update`. [Privacy →](docs/privacy.md)

Apache-2.0


<!-- source: docs/getting-started.md -->

# Getting started

Five minutes from install to a report on your own bucket.

## 1. Install

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh   # macOS, Linux
winget install hxddh.oprobe                                                           # Windows
```

Other ways (Homebrew, `.deb`/`.rpm`, `.msi`, `.dmg`, cargo) are in [install.md](install.md). Check it works:

```bash
oprobe --version
```

## 2. The demo

```bash
oprobe demo
```

No account, no flags. oprobe starts an S3-compatible lab inside its own process that answers `503 SlowDown`
above 24 requests in flight and delays 1 in 40 requests by 250 ms, measures it with 32 workers for 8 seconds,
and narrates the result:

1. **What ran** — the workload and its headline numbers.
2. **The verdict** — where the time went, in one sentence.
3. **What oprobe found** — each finding with its evidence, what to do, and a command to check it.
4. **Where the time went** — the shares of operation time, retries, stragglers.
5. **Look closer** — the commands for the full report, the HTML report and the app.

The demo run is saved like any other (`oprobe runs list`).

## 3. Your bucket

Save the bucket as a named target. `target add` runs a quick read-only check (reachability, TLS, clock,
credentials, listing) right away:

```bash
oprobe target add prod s3://my-bucket/oprobe --region eu-west-1
oprobe target add prod s3://my-bucket/oprobe --credentials profile:prod     # an AWS profile
oprobe target add r2 s3://bucket/x --endpoint https://<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com --region auto
oprobe target add gcs gcs://my-bucket/oprobe
oprobe target add az azblob://container/oprobe --endpoint https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net
```

Or run `oprobe run` with no target in a terminal: it lists what it finds on this machine (AWS profiles in
`~/.aws/config` and `~/.aws/credentials`, Google application default credentials, `AZURE_STORAGE_*`
variables), asks for the bucket and saves the target for you.

Then measure:

```bash
oprobe target test prod        # full doctor: also writes, reads and deletes a probe object
oprobe run prod                # 10 s of the parquet preset with 16 workers
oprobe run prod --preset small-files -c 64 -d 30s
oprobe run prod --existing tables/events/        # read-only, on objects that already exist
oprobe run prod --dry-run                        # the plan: requests, bytes, cost, ETA; sends nothing
```

`oprobe run` writes its test data under `<prefix>/oprobe-run-<id>/` and deletes it at the end (verified).
`--read-only` or `--existing PREFIX` never write. Budgets stop a run early: `--max-cost-usd 0.50`,
`--max-requests 100000`, `--max-bytes 10GiB`, `--max-duration 5m`.

## 4. Read the result

The run prints at most 20 lines: verdict, top findings, key numbers and the command for the full report.

```bash
oprobe runs show                       # the last run, full report (80 columns)
oprobe runs show last --detail         # every column, the timeline, the 5 slowest operations
oprobe runs show last -o html > r.html # charts and every request, one offline file
oprobe runs open last                  # in the app
```

[Reading the report](reading-the-report.md) walks through every section.

## 5. Act on it

```bash
oprobe tune prod --emit-profile tuned.toml --emit-rust storage.rs    # best knobs below the throttling ceiling
oprobe run prod -c 32 --label after
oprobe compare before after                                          # did it help? (exit 3 on regression)
```

Next: [concepts](concepts.md) (targets, runs, baselines, findings), [workloads](workloads.md),
[the CI gate](ci.md).


<!-- source: docs/concepts.md -->

# Concepts

Four things: **targets** you measure, **runs** that record a measurement, **baselines** you compare against,
and **findings** that explain a run.

## Targets

A target is a named storage endpoint: a URL, options and where its credentials come from. Any command that
takes a target accepts:

- a **name** from the config file (`oprobe target add prod s3://bucket/prefix`);
- a **URL**: `s3://bucket/prefix`, `gcs://bucket`, `azblob://container`, `oss://`, `cos://`, `b2://`,
  `webdav://`, `fs:///path`, `memory://` (with `--endpoint`, `--region`, `--option KEY=VALUE` as needed);
- `lab://SCENARIO`: an S3-compatible server with programmable faults inside oprobe (no credentials).

```toml
# <config dir>/oprobe/config.toml   (oprobe config path · oprobe config edit)
[defaults]
target = "prod"            # used when a command is given none
duration = "30s"

[targets.prod]
url = "s3://my-bucket/oprobe"
region = "eu-west-1"
credentials = "profile:prod"     # env | profile:NAME | anonymous; default: the provider's chain
options = { enable_virtual_host_style = "true" }   # OpenDAL options, checked against the service
```

Every setting has a precedence: flags > `OPROBE_*` environment > target > `[defaults]` > built-in.
`oprobe config show` prints each effective value and where it comes from.

| Command | |
|---|---|
| `oprobe target add NAME URL [--region --endpoint --credentials --option K=V]` | Save (or replace) a target; a quick read-only check follows (`--no-test` skips it). |
| `oprobe target list` / `show NAME` / `rm NAME` | Manage. Secrets in options are never printed. |
| `oprobe target test NAME [--read-only]` | The doctor: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP, clock skew, credentials, list/write/read/stat/delete. |

## Runs

A run is one measurement. It is immutable once finished and saved as one file,
`<data dir>/oprobe/runs/<run-id>.oprobe` (`oprobe config path` shows where; `OPROBE_DATA_DIR` moves it).
The file holds the full resolved configuration, the environment, the report and the trace: one row per
operation and one per backend request (up to 1 000 000 requests, sampled beyond that — aggregates stay exact).

Commands refer to runs with a **RUNREF**:

| RUNREF | Means |
|---|---|
| `20261120-143005-a1b2` | a run id |
| `20261120-14` | a unique id prefix |
| `last`, `last~1`, `last~2` | the newest run, the one before, … |
| `before` | the newest run with that `--label` |
| `./ci/run.oprobe` | a run file anywhere |

| Command | |
|---|---|
| `oprobe runs list [-n N]` | Saved runs: id, label, target, when, window, verdict, ops/s, p99, cost/month. |
| `oprobe runs show [RUNREF] [--detail]` | The full report (`-o html`, `-o md`, `-o json`). |
| `oprobe runs open RUNREF` | Open the run in the app. |
| `oprobe runs export RUNREF --format html\|md\|json\|ndjson\|csv\|har\|otlp` | Export. |
| `oprobe runs rm RUNREF…` | Delete runs. |
| `oprobe runs gc --keep 50 --older-than 30d [--dry-run]` | Delete old runs; runs in a baseline are kept. |

## Baselines

A baseline is a named, rolling set of runs (default: the last 10) that new runs are compared against.

```bash
oprobe run prod --baseline main          # compare against `main`, then add this run to it
oprobe baseline list
oprobe compare --baseline main last      # gate the last run against the baseline
```

`oprobe compare A B` compares two runs directly. A comparison lists every configuration difference first:
a different workload or target fails (the numbers are not comparable), different client knobs are an A/B
comparison, a different host or oprobe version is a warning. Exit code 3 means a regression.

## Findings

A finding is one diagnosis item with:

- a stable **code** (`throttling`, `tail-latency`, `connection-churn`, `server-latency`, …) — `oprobe explain CODE`
  documents it;
- a **severity**: info, warning or critical;
- a one-sentence **cause**;
- **evidence**: the numbers, and references to the operations and time windows that show it;
- **advice**: what to change;
- optionally a **verification**: a concrete command that tests the advice.

The **verdict** sums a run up: `ok`, `review` (worth a look), `attention` (warnings) or `critical`
(critical findings or a breached SLA), with a one-sentence headline of where the time went.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | ok |
| 1 | runtime failure (authentication, network, storage, internal) |
| 2 | usage or configuration error |
| 3 | SLA failed or regression |
| 4 | a budget stopped the run (`--max-cost-usd`, `--max-requests`, `--max-bytes`, `--max-duration`) |
| 5 | safety refusal (e.g. a write under `--read-only`) |
| 130 | interrupted (Ctrl-C); the partial run is saved |

With `-o json` or `-o ndjson`, errors are printed on stdout as `{"type":"error","error":{"code":…}}`
with a stable dotted code such as `auth.denied` or `net.timeout`.


<!-- source: docs/reading-the-report.md -->

# Reading the report

The same report comes in four shapes:

| | Command | For |
|---|---|---|
| Brief | `oprobe run …` (default output) | the answer in ≤ 20 lines, 80 columns |
| Full text | `oprobe runs show [RUNREF] [--detail]` | the terminal, logs |
| HTML | `oprobe runs show RUNREF -o html > report.html` (also `oprobe run … -o html`) | charts, every request, sharing |
| Markdown | `-o md` | PR comments, wikis, job summaries |
| JSON | `-o json` | scripts and agents (`oprobe schema report`) |

## The brief

```text
[CRITICAL] Throttling-bound: the service rejected 3.6% of requests with 429/503;
  ✖ 626 throttled responses (429/503)                   ← cause
    3.57% of requests throttled; 609 retries, 63.02s …  ← evidence
    → Lower `concurrency` / `max_inflight_requests` …   ← advice
    next: oprobe tune prod                              ← a command that checks it (when there is one)
  2114.0 ops/s · 119.2 MiB/s · p50 5.04ms · p99 257ms · errors 0.10%
  626 throttled · $12.40 /month · SLA met
full report: oprobe runs show 20261120-084637-d873
```

The badge is the verdict level: **HEALTHY** (ok), **REVIEW** (worth a look: informational findings, warnings,
a partial run), **ATTENTION** (warning findings), **CRITICAL** (critical findings or a breached SLA). At most
three findings are shown, most severe first; `oprobe explain RUNREF` narrates all of them.

## The full text report

| Section | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| header | oprobe version, run id and label, target, preset, window, workers, client, start time |
| verdict | the badge and one sentence of where the time went |
| KEY NUMBERS | throughput (ops/s, MiB/s read/write), latency p50/p99/p99.9/max, failed operations, throttled responses, the SLA, projected cost |
| FINDINGS | every finding: cause `[code]`, evidence, → advice, `try:` command |
| WHERE THE TIME GOES | the share of total operation wall time per layer (below) |
| OPERATIONS | per workload verb: count, ops/s, p50, p99, max, requests per operation, errors |
| BACKEND REQUESTS | per storage API (`GetObject`, `PutObject`, …): count, share on warm connections, mean TTFB and transfer, p99, status codes |
| CONNECTIONS | protocol, TLS, new connections, reuse, peak in-flight requests, dial p50/p99 per phase |
| BYTES & AMPLIFICATION | logical vs backend bytes, read amplification, over-read, requests per operation, cache, integrity |
| COST | the selected price table, per 1M operations and per month, waste, the same workload elsewhere |
| SLOWEST OPERATION | the worst operation request by request, with its async call stack |
| CLEANUP | test data removed (verified), or what is left and how to remove it |

`--detail` adds every column of the tables, the p99 of each request stage, the mean breakdown per verb, every
remote address, the per-second timeline, the configuration (knobs, workload, options, host, trace sampling) and
the five slowest operations.

### Where the time goes

Each operation's wall time is split exactly (an instant counts once even when requests overlap):

| Layer | Time when … | If it dominates |
|---|---|---|
| queue | requests wait for an in-flight permit or a pooled connection | raise `--max-inflight`, or fewer workers per connection pool |
| cache | the local read cache is looked up | — |
| connect | DNS, TCP, proxy CONNECT and TLS of new connections | connections are not reused, or the proxy/TLS is slow (`oprobe probe`) |
| upload | request bodies are sent | bandwidth or a proxy; bigger `--chunk-size`, more `--io-concurrency` |
| server | waiting for the first byte (server work + one round trip) | the store or the distance to it; more parallelism helps until throttling |
| download | response bodies arrive | bandwidth per stream × streams |
| retry | the retry layer sleeps before the next attempt | throttling or errors: see the findings |
| client | everything else: OpenDAL, signing, CRC, your code | CPU (`client cpu`), tiny objects, verification |

## The HTML report

One file, no network: it can be attached to a ticket, opened offline, printed or saved as PDF.

- **Verdict** — the badge, the headline, tiles for throughput, data rate, p50, p99, failed operations,
  throttled responses and projected cost; SLA, partial-run and sampling notes; warnings.
- **Findings** — cards with severity, code, cause, evidence values, the operations and time windows that show
  it (operation links filter the request table), advice and the verification command.
- **Where the time goes** — the layer shares as one 100% bar (hover for values) and a table; request-stage p99
  and the mean breakdown per operation.
- **Timeline** — operations per second, p50 and p99 latency (log axis) and errors/throttled operations per
  second, one stepped sample per second; hover a column for every value.
- **Latency heatmap** — operations by start time and latency bucket (log), darker = more operations.
  Horizontal bands above the bulk are stragglers; vertical stripes are stalls.
- **Operations** — the full verb and API tables, bytes and amplification.
- **Slowest operations** — up to five waterfalls: each request of the operation on a shared millisecond
  axis, coloured by stage (queue, connect, send, time to first byte, body; grey for retry waits and other
  time); the async call stack below.
- **Requests** — every request row (above 5 000 rows: the slowest operations' requests, failed and slowest
  requests, and an even sample, as the page says). Filter with words or `field:text`, `field=value`,
  `total_ms>100`; pick failed / throttled / cold / retried requests; sort by any column.
- **Network**, **Cost**, **Environment** — connections, TLS/TCP per phase, remote addresses, retries and
  error classes; the cost breakdown and comparison; run, host, target options, workload, requested vs
  effective knobs, cleanup.

The ◐ button switches light/dark (the default follows the system).

## Common verdicts

* **Server latency (TTFB)-bound** — the store, or the round trip to it, dominates. More parallelism helps until
  throttling; compare the TCP connect time to see how much of TTFB is network distance.
* **Throttling-bound** — 429/503 and retry backoff. Lower concurrency or run `oprobe tune` to find the ceiling;
  spread keys over more prefixes.
* **Download/upload-bound** — bandwidth per stream × number of streams; raise `io_concurrency` or
  `chunk_size`, check the NIC and any proxy.
* **Connection setup** — connections are not reused (keep-alive off, bodies not drained, tiny idle pool) or the
  proxy/TLS handshake is slow.
* **Client queue** — requests wait for `max_inflight_requests` permits.
* **Client processing** — CPU, OpenDAL overhead, signing, CRC or your consumer.

Every number is defined in [metrics.md](metrics.md).


<!-- source: docs/metrics.md -->

# Metrics & methodology

oprobe measures; it does not estimate. This page explains exactly what every number means, where
it is captured, and the known limits.

## Where measurements come from

```
 your workload (oprobe workers)
   │  OpScope (task-local, follows the op into OpenDAL background tasks)
   ▼
 OpenDAL operator
   ├─ cache layer          → cache lookups/hits, lookup time
   ├─ retry / timeout / tail-cut layers → retry count, backoff (RetryLayer notify)
   ├─ service (s3, gcs, azblob, …)
   └─ HTTP transport
         default:      OpenDAL's own reqwest client, observed through its extension points
         --microscope: oprobe's instrumented connection pool
         queue → [dns → tcp → proxy CONNECT → tls] → send → ttfb → transfer (+ consumer stall)
```

### Two transports: production fidelity vs. microscope

Tuning results are only useful if they were measured on the client you deploy. By default oprobe
therefore sends every request through **OpenDAL's own HTTP client** — reqwest 0.13 with rustls and
aws-lc-rs, configured exactly as `opendal-http-transport-reqwest` builds it (`reqwest::Client::new()`:
HTTP/1.1, environment proxies, platform certificate verifier, no connect timeout, unlimited idle
connections per host, 90 s idle timeout) — and observes it only through reqwest's public extension
points. The only settings oprobe changes are the ones a knob asks for (`keep_alive = false`,
`http = "h2"`, `--proxy`):

| Signal | How it is captured (default mode) |
|---|---|
| DNS | a timed resolver on the same `getaddrinfo` path as reqwest's default resolver |
| TCP / proxy / TLS | a connector layer times each dial; a delegating TLS session store timestamps the ClientHello, which splits TCP (or TCP + proxy CONNECT) from the TLS handshake; the TLS version comes from the key-schedule labels (no secrets are read) |
| Cold vs warm | the connection's local and remote address (`HttpInfo`): the first request seen on a connection is the cold one and carries that connection's dial — if the dial finished while it waited. A dial that lost hyper's race against an idle connection (and went to the pool) counts as a new connection, but the request that later takes it is warm |
| Send / TTFB / transfer / stall | the request body is handed over in 64 KiB frames and reports when the last one was taken (hyper takes a frame only when it can write, so this is within one frame plus the socket send buffer of the last byte leaving); response headers and body chunks are timed as they arrive and as your code consumes them |
| Cancelled requests | a request dropped before its response (OpenDAL's timeout layer, a tail-cut) is recorded with its elapsed time and a `cancelled` error; a response body dropped before its declared length is recorded with an error |

`--microscope` (or `transport = "microscope"`) switches to oprobe's own pool built on hyper's
low-level HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 connections. It sees more — time spent waiting for a pooled
HTTP/1.1 connection as **queue**, proxy CONNECT separately from TCP, the TLS cipher, raw wire bytes,
the exact connection a dial was made for — but it is a different client:

| Default (OpenDAL's client) | `--microscope` (oprobe's pool) |
|---|---|
| Results transfer to production as-is | Results describe oprobe's pool, not your client |
| Waiting for a pooled connection is part of TTFB | Shown as queue time (HTTP/1.1); waiting for an HTTP/2 stream slot is part of TTFB in both |
| Wire rx / tx not available (reported as 0) | Raw socket bytes incl. TLS and framing |
| TLS version only; the cipher suite is not exposed (reported empty) | TLS version and cipher suite |
| Proxy CONNECT reported together with TCP to the proxy | Proxy CONNECT timed on its own |
| HTTP/1.1 unless `http = "h2"` (OpenDAL builds reqwest without `http2`) | ALPN negotiates h2 for https by default |
| reqwest's pool: no connect timeout, unlimited idle connections per host | 10 s timeout per dial phase, at most 256 idle connections per host |

### Observer effect

`cargo run --release --example overhead` runs the same workload against a local TLS lab through
plain OpenDAL (its default client plus the same timeout/retry layers oprobe applies), oprobe's
default mode and `--microscope`. On a 4-core Linux VM with the lab server in the same process
(medians of 3 × 3 s, repeated twice):

| Workload | plain OpenDAL | oprobe default | `--microscope` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 KiB GETs, 32 concurrent | ~24–25 k ops/s | 9–18 % fewer ops/s | 8–14 % *more* ops/s |
| 4 MiB GETs, 16 concurrent | ~5.7–6.5 GiB/s | within noise (±8 %) | within noise |

Small requests at tens of thousands per second over loopback are the worst case: oprobe's
bookkeeping is ~0.5 µs per operation, and the rest is contention on shared aggregation state when
every request takes microseconds. Against real storage (milliseconds per request) the effect is
negligible. The microscope row is also the reason it is not the default: its pool is 20–29 %
faster than OpenDAL's client on this benchmark, so it would make your storage look faster than
your application will see it.

* **Scope propagation.** A logical operation (e.g. one Parquet query) runs inside an `OpScope`.
  OpenDAL's concurrent readers/writers spawn background tasks; oprobe wraps OpenDAL's executor so
  those tasks inherit the scope. Every request is therefore attributed to the operation that caused
  it, even with `io_concurrency > 1`.
* **In-process backends** (`memory://`, `fs://`) have no HTTP; a bottom layer records each backend
  call's service time instead (shown as `service` / "backend").

## Request stages

For every backend request (columns of the *BACKEND REQUESTS* table):

| Stage | Starts | Ends |
|---|---|---|
| `queue` | `fetch()` called | in-flight permit acquired and a usable connection checked out (excluding dial time) |
| `connect` | — | sum of `dns + tcp + proxy + tls`, only for requests that **dialed** a new connection |
| `dns` | resolver call | addresses returned (to the proxy host when a proxy is used — the proxy resolves the target) |
| `tcp` | `connect()` | SYN/ACK completed |
| `proxy` | `CONNECT host:port` written | `200` received from the egress proxy |
| `tls` | ClientHello | handshake complete (ALPN negotiated) |
| `send` | connection ready | last request byte written to the socket (microscope, HTTP/1.1) / last 64 KiB frame handed to the connection (default client) / handed to the stream (HTTP/2) |
| `ttfb` | request sent | response headers received — server think time + one network round trip |
| `transfer` | headers received | body EOF, **minus** consumer stall |
| `stall` | — | time the body sat idle because the consumer had not polled it (application back-pressure) |

`total = queue + connect + send + ttfb + transfer + stall` for each request.

**HTTP/2 caveat.** Requests share one socket, so socket write timestamps cannot be attributed to a
single stream. On HTTP/2, `send` ends when the request body has been handed to the stream;
flow-controlled transmission of large uploads therefore appears in `ttfb`. Use `--http h1` when you
need to separate upload bandwidth from server latency.

## Operation breakdown ("where the time goes")

Each operation's wall time is split exactly into five parts by sweeping its request intervals and
the retry layer's backoff sleeps:

* **backend** — at least one request is on the network (connect, send, ttfb or transfer);
* **queue** — no request is on the network, but at least one is waiting for a permit/connection;
* **retry** — nothing is on the network or queued, and OpenDAL's `RetryLayer` is sleeping before
  the next attempt (exponential backoff with jitter, 50 ms – 5 s). Throttled or failing runs spend
  most of their time here; this is never counted as client time;
* **cache** — local cache lookups (carved out of the remainder);
* **client** — everything else: OpenDAL processing, request signing, buffering, CRC, your code.

Parallel requests are merged (an instant counts once), so `queue + cache + backend + retry + client`
equals
the measured latency of every single operation. The report then splits *backend* into
connect / upload / server / download in proportion to the measured request-stage totals.

## Latency

* Per-operation latencies go into HDR histograms (3 significant digits, µs resolution).
* Closed loop (`concurrency` workers): latency = actual start → completion.
* Open loop (`rate`): arrivals are scheduled at fixed intervals and latency = **intended** start →
  completion (wrk2-style, no coordinated omission). An arrival that finds all `concurrency` slots
  busy waits in a queue and runs when a slot frees up; its queueing delay is part of its latency, so
  saturation shows up in the percentiles. Arrivals still queued when the window ends, and arrivals
  that fall more than `knobs.timeout` behind schedule (bounded backlog), never start and are
  counted as `missed`. `achieved_rate` = started arrivals ÷ window length.
* Warmup operations, and operations that started before the measurement window, are excluded.

## Throughput window

Rates (ops/s, MiB/s, `achieved_rate`) are computed over the measurement window only: it ends at the
deadline (or when `max_ops` is reached / the run is stopped). Operations that started inside the
window and are still in flight at its end are drained and their latencies and bytes recorded, but
the drain time does not stretch the window, so throughput is not understated. Failed operations
count in ops/s but never in the tuner's objective. A run stopped early with Ctrl-C is marked
`interrupted` in the report.

## Bytes and amplification

| Metric | Definition |
|---|---|
| logical read / write | bytes the workload asked to read / wrote |
| backend down / up | HTTP response / request body bytes |
| wire rx / tx | raw socket bytes incl. TLS records, HTTP framing, proxy handshake (`--microscope` only; 0 with the default client) |
| read amplification | backend down ÷ logical read (cache hits lower it, over-fetch raises it) |
| over-read | backend down ÷ (logical read − cache hit bytes): bytes fetched but never requested |
| write amplification | backend up ÷ logical write (retried uploads raise it) |
| requests per op | backend requests ÷ logical operations |

## Slowest operations and call stacks

The eight slowest operations of the window are kept with their complete request lists. While
operations run, oprobe samples [await-tree](https://github.com/risingwavelabs/await-tree) call
stacks every 20 ms for those slower than the current p90 (≥ 2 ms), including OpenDAL background
sub-tasks — so you can see e.g. `read.full → [sub-task 0] → GetObject → http::dial` for a stuck
operation. OpenDAL's own `AwaitTreeLayer` is deliberately not used: it wraps every call and every
read chunk and cost about 14 % throughput on small requests. Request IDs (`x-amz-request-id`, `x-ms-request-id`, …) are kept for support tickets.

## Error classes

Failed operations are counted per class in `resilience.error_classes`. Every OpenDAL error kind
has its own class (`rate_limited`, `permission_denied`, `not_found`, `config_invalid`,
`unsupported`, `is_a_directory`, `not_a_directory`, `already_exists`, `is_same_file`,
`condition_not_match`, `range_not_satisfied`, `conflict`). OpenDAL's catch-all `Unexpected` is
refined structurally, never by matching the error text (object names and ports contain digits):
the last response status (429/503 → `rate_limited`, 401/403 → `permission_denied`, 5xx →
`server_error`), OpenDAL's timeout and tail-cut layers (`timeout`, `tail_cut`), the typed error
chain (reqwest / hyper / I/O timeouts → `timeout`; refused or failed dials → `connect`), then
OpenDAL's `is_temporary()` (`network`) or `unexpected`.

## Client resources

Process CPU (percent of one core) and RSS are sampled every second. When the load generator uses
more than 80 % of the machine's cores, the diagnosis warns that results may understate what the
storage can deliver.

## Integrity

Generated dataset objects are deterministic and their CRC32C is known; whole-object reads are
verified during the run. A sample of written objects is read back after the run with an untraced
client. Any mismatch is a critical finding and fails `oprobe compare`.

## Trace rows

Besides the aggregates, every run file keeps one row per measured operation (`OpRow`: verb, key, start,
latency, bytes, attempts, the five-part breakdown, error) and one per backend request (`ReqRow`: start,
operation, attempt, storage API, method, status, protocol, connection id and reuse, remote address, every stage
in µs, bytes up/down, request id, Retry-After, error). Up to `max_requests` request rows are kept (default
1 000 000; `OPROBE_MAX_REQUESTS` or `[defaults] max_requests`), reservoir-sampled beyond that: the report says
`sampled: true` with the kept and seen counts, and every aggregate stays exact. The heatmap and the per-remote
table are computed from the rows. `oprobe runs export` writes them as CSV, HAR, NDJSON or OTLP; the HTML report
embeds up to 5 000 of them.

## Only with `--microscope`

These values need oprobe's instrumented pool; with OpenDAL's own client (the default) they are 0, empty or
folded into another stage:

| Field | With the default client |
|---|---|
| `bytes.wire_rx_bytes`, `bytes.wire_tx_bytes` | 0 |
| `connections.cipher`, `network.tls.cipher` | empty |
| queue time waiting for a pooled HTTP/1.1 connection | part of TTFB |
| proxy CONNECT timed separately from TCP | reported together with TCP |
| HTTP/2 negotiated by ALPN | HTTP/1.1 unless `--http h2` |


<!-- source: docs/workloads.md -->

# Workloads & presets

## Presets

`--preset NAME` picks a realistic workload; the dataset is generated under the run prefix and removed at the
end (or use your own objects read-only with `--existing PREFIX`).

| Preset | Models | Dataset | Operation mix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `parquet` (default) | lakehouse scans (Spark, DuckDB, DataFusion) | 8 × 16 MiB | stat + 64 KiB footer read + 4 vectored 512 KiB column-chunk ranges |
| `checkpoint` | AI/ML checkpoints | 2 × 32 MiB | 80 % 32 MiB multipart writes, 20 % full restores |
| `small-files` | many small objects (logs, thumbnails, KV blobs) | 256 × 64 KiB | 60 % whole-object GET, 30 % 64 KiB PUT, 10 % HEAD |
| `metadata` | catalog and listing storms | 512 × 4 KiB in 16 partitions | 40 % LIST, 60 % HEAD |
| `mixed` | general purpose | 32 × 4 MiB | 60 % 1 MiB range reads, 10 % full reads, 20 % 1 MiB writes, 10 % stat |

Shape any preset from the command line: `--objects`, `--object-size`, `--access uniform|zipf:1.1|hotset:0.2/0.8`,
`-d/--duration`, `--warmup`, `--max-ops`, `--rate` (open loop), `-c/--concurrency`, `--io-concurrency`,
`--chunk-size`, `--range-gap`, `--http h1|h2`, `--cache SIZE`, `--retries`, `--tail-cut`. `--dry-run` prints
what a combination will cost before it runs.

## Profiles

A profile is a TOML file describing **what** to benchmark (target), **how** (workload) and **with
which client settings** (knobs), plus the SLA used by `tune` and the volume used to project costs.
`oprobe init --preset parquet > my.toml` prints a fully commented template. Every flag of
`oprobe run` overrides the corresponding profile value.

## Target

```toml
[target]
url = "s3://my-bucket/oprobe"       # s3, gcs, azblob, oss, cos, b2, webdav, fs, memory
# insecure = false                  # skip TLS verification (dev only)
# ca_cert = "corp-ca.pem"           # extra CA bundle
# proxy = "http://proxy:3128"       # or "none"; default: HTTPS_PROXY / HTTP_PROXY / NO_PROXY

[target.options]                    # passed to Apache OpenDAL's service builder
region = "eu-west-1"
# endpoint = "https://minio.internal:9000"
# access_key_id = "${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}"   # ${ENV} references are expanded at runtime
```

Option keys are checked against the OpenDAL service's configuration (its field names and
aliases): a key the service would silently ignore — a typo such as `regin`, or another service's
option — is an error with a "did you mean" suggestion.

Secrets are never written to reports: option keys containing `secret`, `key`, `token`,
`password`, `credential` or `sas` are redacted, and `--emit-profile` writes `${ENV}` placeholders.
Without explicit keys, the backend's usual credential chain is used (e.g. `AWS_*` variables,
`~/.aws`, instance metadata, `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`).

URL forms: `s3://bucket/prefix`, `gcs://bucket/prefix`, `azblob://container/prefix` (set
`account_name`), `oss://bucket`, `cos://bucket`, `b2://bucket`, `webdav[s]://host/path`,
`fs:///absolute/path`, `memory://`.

`r2://bucket/prefix` and `minio://bucket/prefix` are S3 with a provider endpoint and never fall
back to AWS: R2 needs `account_id` (`-o account_id=<ID>`, giving
`https://<ID>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com` with region `auto`) or `--endpoint`; MinIO needs
`--endpoint` (path-style addressing is used). Without them oprobe stops with an error.

## Workload

```toml
[workload]
preset = "parquet"        # parquet | checkpoint | small-files | metadata | mixed
duration = "30s"          # measurement window
warmup = "5s"             # not measured: connections, TLS sessions, caches warm up
access = "zipf:1.1"       # uniform | zipf:<s> | hotset:<fraction>/<probability>
# rate = 500.0            # open-loop arrivals per second (default: closed loop)
# max_ops = 20000         # stop after N measured operations
verify = true             # CRC32C checks
cleanup = true            # delete everything under oprobe-run-*/ at the end
seed = 42                 # deterministic op/key selection

[workload.dataset]
objects = 16
object_size = "64MiB"
partitions = 4            # objects spread over part=NN/ prefixes (used by LIST)
# persist = true          # keep the dataset in oprobe-dataset/<fingerprint>/ for later runs
# existing_prefix = "warehouse/events/"   # read-only benchmark of your own objects
```

### Operation mix

If `[[workload.mix]]` is present it replaces the preset's mix. Each entry has an `op` and a
`weight`:

| `op` | Fields | What it does | Verb in reports |
|---|---|---|---|
| `read` | `size` (optional) | random aligned range of `size`, or the whole object | `read.range` / `read.full` |
| `parquet_scan` | `columns`, `column_size`, `footer_size` | `stat`, footer read, one vectored read of non-overlapping column chunks (coalesced with `range_gap`) | `parquet.scan` |
| `write` | `size` | single PUT | `write` |
| `multipart_write` | `size` | streaming writer, parts of `chunk_size`, `io_concurrency` parts in flight | `write.multipart` |
| `stat` | — | HEAD a dataset object | `stat` |
| `list` | `recursive` | LIST one partition | `list` |

```toml
[[workload.mix]]
op = "read"
size = "256KiB"
weight = 70

[[workload.mix]]
op = "write"
size = "1MiB"
weight = 30
```

Writes go to a bounded set of scratch keys that are overwritten, so long runs do not grow storage
without bound. Writes are skipped automatically for `existing_prefix` datasets.

## Knobs

```toml
[knobs]
concurrency = 16            # concurrent operations (closed loop) / in-flight cap (open loop)
io_concurrency = 4          # OpenDAL reader/writer .concurrent(n)
chunk_size = "8MiB"         # reader/writer .chunk(n); multipart part size
range_gap = "64KiB"         # reader .gap(n): merge ranges closer than this
max_inflight_requests = 0   # cap on concurrent HTTP requests (0 = unlimited)
http_version = "auto"       # auto | h1 | h2
keep_alive = true
cache = false               # in-memory byte-bounded LRU read cache
cache_size = "256MiB"
retries = 3                 # RetryLayer attempts (jittered exponential backoff)
tail_cut = false            # TailCutLayer: cancel & retry stragglers above adaptive p95
timeout = "60s"
```

## SLA and cost

```toml
[sla]                       # `oprobe run` / `tune` exit 3 when the result breaches it
enforce = true              # false (or `--sla none`): report the verdict, never fail on it
max_error_rate = 0.01       # default: at most 1% failed operations
p99_ms = 250.0              # worst per-operation p99 (unset: no latency objective)
max_throttle_rate = 0.0     # throttled-operation share (unset: `run` ignores throttling that
                            # retries absorb; `tune` treats any 429/503 as infeasible)
```

Corrupted data (a CRC32C mismatch on read-back) always breaches the SLA. Every SLA field can also
be set from the command line: `--max-error-rate 1%`, `--max-throttle-rate 0%`, `--p99-ms 250`,
`--sla none`.

```toml
[cost]
provider = "aws-s3"         # pricing preset; default: detected from the endpoint
monthly_ops = 100000000     # projection volume
stored_gib = 1024
egress_fraction = 0.0       # share of downloads that leave the cloud
# [cost.pricing]            # custom prices override the preset
```

See [cost.md](cost.md) for the pricing model.


<!-- source: docs/ci.md -->

# CI: the storage regression gate

Measure storage on every change, compare it with a baseline and fail on regression — with the GitHub Action,
or with two commands anywhere else.

## GitHub Action

```yaml
# .github/workflows/storage.yml
name: storage
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write      # the sticky comment
  id-token: write           # only for cloud credentials via OIDC (below)

jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4     # or google-github-actions/auth, azure/login
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/oprobe-ci
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - uses: hxddh/oprobe@v3
        with:
          target: s3://ci-bucket/oprobe
          preset: small-files
          duration: 20s
          args: -c 16 --max-cost-usd 0.25
          baseline: main            # a name: kept in the Actions cache, refreshed by pushes to main
```

What it does:

1. installs the pinned oprobe release (`version`, default the release that matches the action tag) after
   checking its SHA-256 against the release's `SHA256SUMS`;
2. `oprobe run TARGET` with the preset, duration and extra `args`, labelled with the commit SHA;
3. compares the run with the baseline (`oprobe compare`), writing Markdown and JUnit;
4. writes the comparison and the report to the job summary;
5. uploads an artifact with the `.oprobe` run file, `oprobe-report.html`, `oprobe-report.md` and the gate
   files — open the run later with `oprobe runs show oprobe-report/<id>.oprobe` or `oprobe runs open …`;
6. posts one pull-request comment and updates it on every push (it finds its own comment by a marker);
7. fails the step on a regression (exit 3) or when the run breaches its SLA (`fail-on-regression: false`
   only reports).

### Inputs

| Input | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `target` | — | URL or configured name; `memory://` and `lab://demo` need no credentials |
| `version` | the action's release | `latest` follows new releases |
| `preset`, `duration` | preset's default, `20s` | |
| `args` | | extra `oprobe run` flags (`-c 32`, `--region`, budgets, `--existing PREFIX`, …) |
| `baseline` | | a `.oprobe` / report `.json` path in the workspace, or a **name** stored in the Actions cache |
| `update-baseline` | `auto` | replace a named baseline with this run: `auto` = pushes to the default branch that passed; `true` / `false` |
| `compare-args` | | e.g. `--max-p99-increase 30 --allow-throttling` |
| `fail-on-regression` | `true` | |
| `comment` | `true` | sticky PR comment (needs `pull-requests: write`) |
| `artifact-name` | `oprobe-report` | also distinguishes comments when the action runs more than once |

Outputs: `run-id`, `run-file`, `html-report`, `run-exit-code`, `regression`.

### Baselines

- **A name** (`baseline: main`): the first passing push to the default branch stores its run in the Actions
  cache; later runs compare against it, and every passing push to the default branch replaces it. Pull
  requests never replace it.
- **A file** (`baseline: benchmarks/baseline.oprobe`): commit a run file (or download one from an earlier
  artifact) and compare against it. Refresh it on purpose: `oprobe run … && cp <run file> benchmarks/`.

## Any CI

```bash
oprobe run "$TARGET" --preset small-files -d 20s --label "$COMMIT" --non-interactive
oprobe compare baseline.oprobe last --markdown gate.md --junit gate.xml   # exit 3 on regression
oprobe runs show last -o html > report.html
```

The run is saved under `$OPROBE_DATA_DIR` (set it to a cached directory to keep history and baselines between
jobs). In scripts, prefer `-o json` (one document) or `-o ndjson` (events, then the result).

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | ok |
| 1 | runtime failure (credentials, network, storage) |
| 2 | usage or configuration error |
| 3 | SLA breached (`run`), regression (`compare`), or `--fail-on` matched |
| 4 | a budget stopped the run |
| 5 | safety refusal (`--read-only`) |
| 130 | interrupted |

The default SLA of `oprobe run`: at most 1% failed operations and no corrupted data. Tighten it with
`--max-error-rate 0.1%`, `--max-throttle-rate 0%`, `--p99-ms 250`; `--sla none` reports without failing;
`--fail-on warning|critical` also fails on findings of that severity.

## What the gate checks

| Check | Default limit | Flag |
|---|---|---|
| same workload (preset, mix, dataset, access, rate, verify, seed) | must be identical | `--allow-workload-change` |
| same target (scheme, bucket/prefix, endpoint, options) | must be identical | `--allow-target-change` |
| throughput (ops/s, MiB/s) | −10 % | `--max-throughput-drop` |
| p50 per operation | +20 % and > 1 ms | `--max-p50-increase`, `--min-latency-delta-ms` |
| p99 per operation | +20 % and > 1 ms | `--max-p99-increase` |
| failed operations | +0.5 percentage points | `--max-error-increase` |
| new 429/503 throttling | not allowed | `--allow-throttling` |
| CRC32C corruption | must be 0 | always |
| requests per operation | +10 % | `--max-request-amp-increase` |
| read amplification | +10 % | `--max-read-amp-increase` |
| cost per 1M operations (when a price table applies to both) | +10 % | `--max-cost-increase` |

Operations with fewer than `--min-samples` (30) samples are skipped for latency checks. Every setting that
differs is listed first: a different workload or target fails (not comparable), different client knobs are
an A/B comparison, a different host, proxy or oprobe version is a warning.

## Keeping it stable

* Use `--max-ops` with an open-loop `--rate` (see `profiles/ci-gate.toml`): every run issues the same
  operation sequence (fixed seed) at the same arrival rate.
* Run baseline and candidate on the same runner class; shared runners are noisy, so keep latency limits wider
  than throughput limits.
* `memory://` and `fs://` gate client-side regressions (OpenDAL usage, request amplification); gate network
  behaviour against a dedicated bucket or `lab://`.
* Budgets keep a misconfigured job cheap: `--max-cost-usd`, `--max-requests`, `--max-duration`.


<!-- source: docs/agents.md -->

# oprobe for agents

oprobe is built to be driven by programs and AI agents as well as people. Everything a person
sees has a machine form with a published JSON Schema, every failure has a stable error code and
exit code, every run is stored and addressable, and the whole tool is available as an MCP server.

This page is for agents (and their authors) **using** oprobe. Agents working **on** the oprobe
repository should read [`AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md).

## Contracts

| What | Where | Schema |
|---|---|---|
| Command results | `-o json` (one document on stdout) | `oprobe schema <command>` |
| Live events | `-o ndjson` (one event per line, ends with `result` or `error`) | `oprobe schema events` |
| Errors | `{"type":"error","error":{code,message,hint?,retryable,docs?}}` on stdout in json/ndjson modes | `oprobe schema error` |
| Report v3 | `report` of `run`, `runs show`, MCP `get_run` | `oprobe schema report` |
| Run files | `runs/<id>.oprobe` (zstd NDJSON: header, report, op rows, req rows) | `oprobe schema run-file` |
| Config | `config.toml` (`[defaults]`, `[targets.NAME]`) | `oprobe schema config` |
| Self-description | `oprobe capabilities -o json` | `oprobe schema capabilities` |

Schemas are JSON Schema 2020-12 with `$id`
`https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/schemas/3/<name>.json`; the checked-in copies live in
[`schemas/`](../schemas). `oprobe schema` lists every name.

Rules that hold everywhere:

- stdout carries only the result; logs and progress go to stderr (or become `log` events).
- Numeric field names carry their unit (`_us`, `_ms`, `_s`, `_bytes`, `_per_s`, `_pct`, `_ratio`,
  `_usd`, `_count`); enums are lowercase `snake_case`; there are no human-formatted numbers in
  machine fields.
- Consumers must ignore unknown fields and unknown event types.

### Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | ok |
| 1 | runtime failure (auth, network, storage, internal) |
| 2 | usage or configuration error |
| 3 | SLA failed or regression (`compare`) |
| 4 | a budget stopped the run (the partial run is saved) |
| 5 | a safety rail refused the command |
| 130 | interrupted |

`oprobe capabilities -o json` lists every error code with its exit code and whether retrying can
help (`retryable`).

### Run references

Commands and tools that take a run accept a RUNREF: the run id (`20261120-143005-a1b2`), a unique
id prefix, `last`, `last~N`, a label, or a path to a `.oprobe` file.

## Safe workflow

1. **Know the tool**: `oprobe capabilities -o json` (services, presets, providers, error and
   finding codes, MCP tools, defaults).
2. **Preflight**: `oprobe doctor TARGET -o json` — `ready` must be true. Add `--read-only` to
   skip the write/read/delete probe.
3. **Plan**: `oprobe run TARGET … --dry-run -o json` — requests, bytes, objects written and
   deleted, cost and ETA. Nothing is sent to the target.
4. **Run with budgets**: `oprobe run TARGET … --max-requests N --max-duration 2m
   --max-cost-usd 0.10 -o ndjson`. A breached budget stops the run (exit 4, `safety.budget_exceeded`)
   and still saves the partial run. `--read-only` refuses anything that writes (exit 5);
   `--existing PREFIX` benchmarks existing objects and never writes.
5. **Explain**: `oprobe explain last -o json` — verdict, findings with evidence and documentation,
   outlier attribution of the slowest 1 % of requests, suggested next commands.
6. **Change one knob, run again, compare**: `oprobe compare last~1 last -o json` (exit 3 on a
   regression).

Writes are always confined to `<prefix>/oprobe-run-<id>/` and removed when the run ends;
`oprobe cleanup TARGET --dry-run` finds leftovers of killed runs. `memory://` needs no
credentials and never leaves the process — use it to learn the outputs.

## MCP server

`oprobe mcp` serves the Model Context Protocol on stdio; `oprobe mcp --http 127.0.0.1:8765`
serves Streamable HTTP at `http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp`.

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| (default) | read-only: runs that would upload a dataset or write are refused with `safety.read_only` (`memory://` and `existing` runs are allowed); `doctor` skips its write probe; `cleanup` is a dry run |
| `--allow-write` | enable runs that write test data, `start_tune`, `cleanup` with `confirm` |
| `--max-cost-usd`, `--max-requests`, `--max-bytes`, `--max-duration` | budgets applied to every run the server starts (a call can only lower them) |
| `--allow-target NAME\|URL-PREFIX` | only these targets (repeatable; prefixes match at `/` boundaries) |
| `--max-concurrent-runs N` | runs executing at once (others queue; default 1) |

### Tools

`tools/list` order is fixed. Every tool has an `inputSchema` and an `outputSchema`, returns
`structuredContent` plus a one-paragraph text summary, and reports failures as tool errors
(`isError: true`) whose second text block is the JSON error document.

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `doctor` | preflight a target |
| `probe_endpoint` | DNS/TCP/TLS handshakes and cold/warm TTFB of an endpoint |
| `plan_run` | dry-run plan, effective budgets, `allowed` + `refusals` |
| `start_run` | start a run in the background; returns the run id at once (`wait: true` blocks); progress notifications when the call has a `progressToken` |
| `get_run` | status, progress and (when done) summary and report; also any stored RUNREF |
| `cancel_run` | stop a run (cleanup runs, the partial run is saved) |
| `list_runs` | stored runs and runs this server started |
| `explain_run` | narrated explanation (same as `oprobe explain RUNREF`) |
| `analyze_run` | outlier attribution for a `Selection` (time window, latency floor, API) or the slowest N % |
| `compare_runs` | regression gate between two runs |
| `start_tune` | throttle-aware tuning in the background |
| `estimate_cost` | request cost at list prices vs the cost budget |
| `cleanup` | leftover test data (dry run unless `confirm` on a write-enabled server) |
| `list_targets` | configured targets, what is allowed, server budgets |

Resources: `oprobe://runs/{id}/report`, `oprobe://runs/{id}/events` (NDJSON), `oprobe://runs/{id}/slowest`,
`oprobe://runs/{id}/html` (Markdown until the HTML renderer lands), `oprobe://schema/{name}`,
`oprobe://docs/{getting-started|safety|findings|finding/CODE}`, `oprobe://presets`.

Prompts: `diagnose-slow-reads`, `tune-for-p99`, `ci-gate-setup`.

### Setup

Claude Code:

```sh
claude mcp add oprobe -- oprobe mcp --max-requests 50000 --max-duration 2m
# allow writes to a scratch bucket only:
claude mcp add oprobe-rw -- oprobe mcp --allow-write --allow-target s3://scratch-bucket/oprobe/ --max-cost-usd 0.50
```

Claude Desktop (`claude_desktop_config.json`), Cursor (`.cursor/mcp.json`) and other clients that
use the `mcpServers` format:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "oprobe": {
      "command": "oprobe",
      "args": ["mcp", "--max-requests", "50000", "--max-duration", "2m"],
      "env": { "AWS_PROFILE": "bench" }
    }
  }
}
```

VS Code (`.vscode/mcp.json`):

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "oprobe": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "oprobe",
      "args": ["mcp", "--max-requests", "50000"]
    }
  }
}
```

Streamable HTTP (any client): start `oprobe mcp --http 127.0.0.1:8765` and point the client at
`http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp`. Only loopback `Host` headers are accepted unless you bind another
address.

Credentials come from the server's environment (the usual provider chains, `AWS_PROFILE`, …) or
from configured targets (`oprobe target add`); never pass secrets as tool arguments.

## Explaining findings

`oprobe explain CODE` documents a finding code; `oprobe explain --list` lists them. The catalog
below is generated from the same source (`src/mcp/catalog.rs`).

<!-- BEGIN finding-codes (generated: OPROBE_BLESS=1 cargo test --test agent) -->

<a id="finding-integrity"></a>
### `integrity` — Data read back differs from data written

CRC32C verification of objects oprobe wrote and read back failed: the storage path returned different bytes. *(correctness, usually critical)*

- **Causes:** a proxy or gateway that rewrites or truncates bodies; multipart parts assembled in the wrong order by an S3-compatible service; a storage service bug or degraded node
- **Verify:** report.integrity.corrupted > 0; repeat with `oprobe run TARGET --preset checkpoint` and compare integrity counts; run `oprobe compat TARGET` for multipart and checksum edge cases
- **Knobs:** --no-verify (disables the check; never to hide this); --chunk-size; --proxy

<a id="finding-errors"></a>
### `errors` — Operations failed

Some logical operations failed after retries; critical when the failure rate exceeds the SLA's max error rate. *(availability, usually warning)*

- **Causes:** missing permissions (403) or wrong credentials; objects or buckets that do not exist (404); timeouts or connection resets on an overloaded path; throttling that outlasts the retry budget
- **Verify:** report.resilience.error_classes and report.summary.error_ratio; `oprobe doctor TARGET` for credentials, permissions and the endpoint; `oprobe analyze RUNREF --where error` / MCP analyze_run to see which requests failed
- **Knobs:** --retries; --max-error-rate; --concurrency

<a id="finding-throttling"></a>
### `throttling` — The service rate-limited requests (429/503)

The storage service answered with 429 or 503 SlowDown: the request rate is above what the bucket, prefix or account allows right now. *(availability, usually critical)*

- **Causes:** too many concurrent requests against one prefix (S3 partitions scale per prefix); a request-rate quota on the account or bucket; a burst right after the bucket was created (not yet scaled out)
- **Verify:** report.resilience.throttled_responses and the retry share in report.stages.shares.retry_pct; re-run with half the concurrency and compare (`oprobe compare`); `oprobe tune TARGET` finds the throttling ceiling
- **Knobs:** --concurrency; --max-inflight; --retries; --max-throttle-rate

<a id="finding-client-queue"></a>
### `client-queue` — Operations wait for in-flight request permits

Operations spend most of their time queued in the client before a request is even sent. *(bottleneck, usually warning)*

- **Causes:** max_inflight_requests caps requests below concurrency × io_concurrency; a connection pool that is too small
- **Verify:** report.stages.shares.queue_pct is the largest share; report.stages.request_p99.queue_ms; re-run with `--max-inflight 0` and compare
- **Knobs:** --max-inflight; --concurrency; --io-concurrency

<a id="finding-client-cpu"></a>
### `client-cpu` — Load generator CPU is saturated

The machine running oprobe is near its CPU limit, so measurements understate what the storage can do. *(client, usually warning)*

- **Causes:** CRC32C verification of large objects; TLS on many connections from a small machine; very small operations at high concurrency
- **Verify:** report.client (CPU use vs cores); re-run with `--no-verify` or fewer workers and compare throughput
- **Knobs:** --no-verify; --concurrency; --object-size

<a id="finding-consumer-stall"></a>
### `consumer-stall` — Response bodies wait for the consumer

Data arrives faster than the application side consumes it; storage is not the limit. *(client, usually warning)*

- **Causes:** slow decoding or copying of downloaded data; a CPU-bound consumer
- **Verify:** report.stages.request_p99.stall_ms larger than body_ms; MCP analyze_run: `stage=stall` over-represented among slow requests
- **Knobs:** --io-concurrency; --chunk-size

<a id="finding-client-overhead"></a>
### `client-overhead` — Time is spent outside network requests

Most operation time is client-side processing (signing, buffering, OpenDAL, CRC), not network requests. *(client, usually info)*

- **Causes:** in-memory or local backends (expected); tiny objects where per-operation overhead dominates
- **Verify:** report.stages.shares.client_pct is the largest share
- **Knobs:** --object-size; --no-verify

<a id="finding-connect"></a>
### `connect` — Connection setup dominates

DNS, TCP, proxy and TLS handshakes take most of the operation time: connections are not reused. *(network, usually warning)*

- **Causes:** keep-alive disabled; response bodies not fully drained, so connections are not returned to the pool; an idle pool too small for the concurrency; a proxy that closes connections
- **Verify:** report.connections (reuse ratio, dialed count) and report.network.tcp / tls; MCP analyze_run: `connection=cold` over-represented among slow requests; `oprobe probe ENDPOINT` for handshake times
- **Knobs:** --no-keep-alive (remove it); --http h2; --microscope

<a id="finding-server-latency"></a>
### `server-latency` — Latency-bound on server time-to-first-byte

Requests spend most of their time waiting for the server's first byte; throughput scales with parallelism. *(bottleneck, usually info)*

- **Causes:** network round trips to a distant region; per-request service latency of the storage (normal for object stores); many small range reads that could be coalesced
- **Verify:** report.stages.request_p99.ttfb_ms dominates; `oprobe probe ENDPOINT` cold vs warm TTFB; re-run with higher `--concurrency` and compare throughput
- **Knobs:** --concurrency; --io-concurrency; --range-gap; --region

<a id="finding-download-bound"></a>
### `download-bound` — Bandwidth-bound on downloads

Transferring response bodies dominates; the per-stream or aggregate bandwidth is the limit. *(bottleneck, usually info)*

- **Causes:** NIC, VM or proxy bandwidth caps; cross-region or internet links; too few parallel streams for large objects
- **Verify:** report.stages.shares.download_pct is the largest share; report.summary (MiB/s) against the machine's network limit
- **Knobs:** --io-concurrency; --concurrency; --chunk-size

<a id="finding-upload-bound"></a>
### `upload-bound` — Bandwidth-bound on uploads

Sending request bodies dominates; upload bandwidth is the limit. *(bottleneck, usually info)*

- **Causes:** NIC, VM or proxy bandwidth caps; single-stream uploads of large objects
- **Verify:** report.stages.shares.upload_pct is the largest share
- **Knobs:** --io-concurrency; --chunk-size; --concurrency

<a id="finding-retry-backoff"></a>
### `retry-backoff` — Operations spend their time waiting to retry

Requests fail with temporary errors (not throttling) and operations sleep between retry attempts. *(availability, usually warning)*

- **Causes:** timeouts or connection resets; 5xx errors from an unhealthy service; a too aggressive timeout
- **Verify:** report.stages.shares.retry_pct and report.resilience; MCP analyze_run: `attempt=retry` and `error=…` among slow requests
- **Knobs:** --retries; --tail-cut

<a id="finding-local-backend"></a>
### `local-backend` — Local backend service time dominates

An in-process backend (memory, fs) is measured: results reflect local disk or memory, not network storage. *(bottleneck, usually info)*

- **Causes:** benchmarking memory:// or fs:// (expected)
- **Verify:** report.target.scheme is memory or fs

<a id="finding-connection-churn"></a>
### `connection-churn` — Connections are rarely reused

Many requests open a new connection even though connection setup is not (yet) the main bottleneck. *(network, usually warning)*

- **Causes:** keep-alive disabled or ignored by a proxy; response bodies not drained; a pool smaller than the concurrency
- **Verify:** report.connections: dialed count vs requests; MCP analyze_run: `connection=cold` lift among slow requests
- **Knobs:** --no-keep-alive (remove it); --http h2; --max-inflight

<a id="finding-slow-tls"></a>
### `slow-tls` — Slow TLS handshakes

TLS handshakes take over 100 ms at the median. *(network, usually info)*

- **Causes:** a long round trip to the endpoint; a TLS-inspecting proxy; no session resumption
- **Verify:** report.network.tls.handshake; `oprobe probe ENDPOINT` (handshake breakdown, proxy)
- **Knobs:** --http h2; --proxy

<a id="finding-overread"></a>
### `overread` — Downloaded bytes were never requested

Range coalescing or chunking downloaded noticeably more bytes than the application asked for, costing egress and bandwidth. *(efficiency, usually warning)*

- **Causes:** a large range_gap merging distant ranges; a chunk size larger than the reads
- **Verify:** report.bytes (overread ratio, backend bytes down)
- **Knobs:** --range-gap; --chunk-size

<a id="finding-cache-ineffective"></a>
### `cache-ineffective` — The read cache rarely hits

The in-memory read cache is enabled but almost every lookup misses. *(efficiency, usually info)*

- **Causes:** an access pattern with little reuse; a working set larger than the cache
- **Verify:** report.cache (lookups, hits, hit ratio)
- **Knobs:** --cache SIZE; --access zipf:1.1

<a id="finding-tail-latency"></a>
### `tail-latency` — p99 latency is far above the median

An operation's p99 is more than 5× its median: a minority of requests are much slower. *(bottleneck, usually warning)*

- **Causes:** server stragglers; cold connections or retries on a few requests; throttling bursts; a slow remote IP behind the endpoint
- **Verify:** report.slowest op ids and their request rows; `oprobe explain RUNREF` / MCP analyze_run with the slowest 1 % selected
- **Knobs:** --tail-cut; --retries; --concurrency

<a id="finding-sla-p99"></a>
### `sla-p99` — p99 latency exceeds the SLA

An operation's p99 is above the `--p99-ms` objective. *(sla, usually warning)*

- **Causes:** queueing or throttling at this concurrency; tail latency of the service
- **Verify:** report.verbs[].latency vs report.sla.p99_ms
- **Knobs:** --p99-ms; --concurrency; oprobe tune --objective latency

<a id="finding-rate-not-sustained"></a>
### `rate-not-sustained` — The target arrival rate was not sustained

With an open-loop `--rate`, arrivals queued behind busy workers; their wait is part of the measured latency. *(client, usually warning)*

- **Causes:** too few workers (`--concurrency`) for the rate; a rate above what the target can serve
- **Verify:** report.open_loop (target vs achieved rate, missed arrivals)
- **Knobs:** --rate; --concurrency

<!-- END finding-codes -->


<!-- source: docs/tuning.md -->

# Tuning

`oprobe tune` searches for the best client configuration **by measuring**, not by modelling. It
prepares the dataset once and then runs short trials (default 5 s + 1 s warmup) with different
knobs against the real target.

```bash
oprobe tune s3://bucket/oprobe --preset parquet --p99-ms 250 \
  --emit-profile tuned.toml --emit-rust storage.rs --emit-python storage.py --json tune.json
```

## Search strategy

1. **Baseline** — your current knobs.
2. **Concurrency ladder** — 2, 4, 8, … up to `--max-concurrency`. The ladder stops at the first
   trial that receives a 429/503 (the *throttling ceiling*), violates the SLA, or stops improving
   (two consecutive steps below +5 %).
3. **Ceiling refinement** — binary search between the last clean level and the ceiling.
   After every throttled trial the tuner pauses (`--cooldown`, or longer if that trial received
   `Retry-After`, capped at 60 s; `Retry-After` is honored even with `--cooldown 0`) so the next
   trial is not measured against a depleted rate limiter. Ctrl-C interrupts the pause.
4. **Safety margin** — the recommended concurrency is capped at 80 % of the ceiling to leave
   headroom for production variance (a trial at the cap is run when the best clean trial lies
   above it). The notes state the ceiling once — the throttled level the bisection ended on and
   the highest clean level — and explain the margin with numbers, e.g. "concurrency 12 was clean
   and measured +21 % but sits only 8 % below the ceiling, so it was not recommended".
5. **Workload-specific knobs** — coordinate descent over only the knobs that matter for the mix:
   `chunk_size` and `io_concurrency` for multipart writes and large reads, `range_gap` for vectored
   (Parquet) reads, the read cache for skewed access (or uniform access over your real objects with
   `existing_prefix` when they fit), and HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 for HTTPS. A cache win that relies on
   the whole generated test dataset fitting in the cache is flagged as dataset-size-dependent.
   A change is accepted only if it improves the objective by more than 3 % (noise guard).
   For multipart writes, chunk candidates are clamped to the service's part-size limits first
   (OpenDAL raises a write chunk to `write_multi_min_size`, 5 MiB on S3/GCS), so the tuner never
   recommends a chunk OpenDAL would not use. Every report records the chunk that was actually
   written with under `effective_knobs` (requested vs effective) and warns when they differ.
6. **Confirmation** — the winner runs again for twice the trial duration; the report you get is
   from that run.

A trial is *feasible* when its error rate, throttle rate and worst per-operation p99 satisfy
`[sla]`. Infeasible trials are never chosen if a feasible one exists. If none is feasible, the
tuner reports "no trial met the SLA" and picks the least-bad trial (not throttled if possible,
then the lowest error rate). The objective throughput counts successful operations only.

## Objectives

| `--objective` | Picks |
|---|---|
| `throughput` (default) | highest MiB/s (or ops/s for small-object workloads) |
| `latency` | lowest worst-case p99 among configs within 80 % of the best throughput |
| `cost` | lowest cost per million operations among configs within 80 % of the best throughput |

## Outputs

* `--emit-profile` — your profile with the winning `[knobs]`; run it with `oprobe run --profile`.
* `--emit-rust` — an OpenDAL 0.59 `Operator` builder that reproduces exactly the measured client:
  `TimeoutLayer` (operation + I/O timeout), `TailCutLayer` (when enabled) and `RetryLayer`
  (jittered exponential backoff, 50 ms – 5 s) with the parameters oprobe applied, an HTTP
  concurrency limit only when `max_inflight_requests` was set, a custom reqwest client only when
  the knobs changed OpenDAL's default one (keep-alive off, HTTP/2), and reader/writer helpers with
  the tuned chunk/gap/concurrency (the writer chunk is the part size OpenDAL actually used). Both
  the measured operator and the generated code are derived from one `ClientStack` value, and a
  test rebuilds the layers from the generated source and compares them parameter for parameter.
* `--emit-python` — the same for the `opendal` Python package where the binding allows
  (`RetryLayer` with identical parameters); measured layers the binding cannot express (timeouts,
  tail cut, HTTP limit) are listed in the header instead of being approximated.
* `--json` — the full report of the confirmation run plus every trial (`tune.trials`).

With the default text format, everything that is part of the result — the trial table, the
recommendation and the confirmation report — goes to stdout; stderr only carries progress
(dataset upload, cool-down pauses). With `-o json|md`, stdout holds only that
document and the trial table is shown on stderr as progress.

## Budget

`--max-trials` (default 24) bounds the number of trials (the final confirmation run comes on
top); with 5 s trials the typical run takes
1–3 minutes. Use `--trial-duration 15s` for noisy networks. Every trial uses the same dataset;
the test data is removed at the end.


<!-- source: docs/cost.md -->

# Cost model

oprobe prices **what it measured**, scaled to the volume you declare. No traffic model is assumed.

1. **Per-operation usage** from the measurement window: backend requests per logical operation
   by billing class, bytes downloaded and uploaded per operation, failed/throttled requests,
   over-read bytes, and GETs/bytes served by the cache.
2. **Billing class** of each request comes from the real request line:

   | Class | APIs |
   |---|---|
   | write | PutObject, CreateMultipartUpload, UploadPart, CompleteMultipartUpload, CopyObject |
   | list | ListObjects (S3 ListObjectsV2, GCS objects.list, Azure List Blobs, B2 list_file_names) |
   | read | GetObject, HeadObject, other GETs |
   | delete | DeleteObject(s), AbortMultipartUpload |
   | free | control-plane calls (e.g. B2 authorize / get_upload_url) |

3. **Projection**: `monthly cost = per-op usage × [cost].monthly_ops × prices + stored GB × storage price`.
   Internet egress applies only to the `egress_fraction` of downloaded bytes (default 0: compute
   in the same region).

## When cost is projected

A price table is applied only when it is known to be the right one:

* the endpoint is a recognised cloud storage endpoint (`*.amazonaws.com`,
  `storage.googleapis.com`, `*.blob.core.windows.net`, `*.r2.cloudflarestorage.com`,
  `*.backblazeb2.com`, `*.aliyuncs.com`, or the scheme's implied endpoint for `gcs`, `azblob`,
  `oss`, `b2`), or
* the profile chose one explicitly (`[cost].provider` / `--provider`, or `[cost.pricing]`).

Everything else — `memory://`, `fs://`, localhost, private addresses, MinIO, Ceph or any unknown
endpoint — gets no projection: the report's `cost.applicable` is `false` with a
`not_applicable_reason`, the terminal report omits the COST section, `oprobe compare` skips the cost
check, and `oprobe tune --objective cost` refuses to run. The measured per-operation usage
(`cost.per_op`) is still reported.

## Price presets (list prices, as of 2025-06)

| Key | Storage $/GB-mo | Write $/M | List $/M | Read $/M | Egress $/GB |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `aws-s3` | 0.023 | 5.00 | 5.00 | 0.40 | 0.09 |
| `gcs` | 0.020 | 5.00 | 5.00 | 0.40 | 0.12 |
| `azure-blob` | 0.0184 | 6.50 | 6.50 | 0.50 | 0.087 |
| `cloudflare-r2` | 0.015 | 4.50 | 4.50 | 0.36 | 0 |
| `backblaze-b2` | 0.006 | 0 | 4.00 | 0.40 | 0.01 |
| `aliyun-oss` | 0.017 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.074 |

Prices change and differ by region, tier and contract: override them.

```toml
[cost]
monthly_ops = 250000000
stored_gib = 20480
egress_fraction = 0.1

[cost.pricing]
provider = "S3 (our EDP rate)"
storage_gb_month = 0.018
write_per_million = 4.0
list_per_million = 4.0
read_per_million = 0.32
egress_per_gb = 0.05
```

## Waste and savings

* **failed/throttled requests** — requests that returned 429/503/5xx/4xx (except 404) or failed on
  the network, priced at the average request price; most providers bill them and they add no value.
* **over-read egress** — bytes downloaded but not requested (range coalescing, chunked reads).
* **cache savings** — GETs and bytes the local cache answered instead of the backend.

The comparison table applies the same measured usage to every preset, answering "what would this
exact workload cost on R2 / GCS / B2?". Latency and throughput of other providers are not implied —
measure them with `oprobe run` against each provider.


<!-- source: docs/install.md -->

# Installing oprobe

## Quick

| Platform | Command |
|---|---|
| macOS, Linux | `curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh \| sh` |
| Windows | `winget install hxddh.oprobe` |
| Windows (no winget) | `irm https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 \| iex` |
| Rust ≥ 1.97 | `cargo install oprobe --locked` (`--features gui` adds the window on Linux; needs `libgtk-4-dev`) |

The install scripts download the archive for your platform, verify it against `SHA256SUMS` and put `oprobe`
in `~/.local/bin` (`OPROBE_INSTALL_DIR` to change). Update later with `oprobe self-update`.

## Release assets

Every release publishes the same program in each platform's native format:

| Asset | Platform |
|---|---|
| `oprobe-<ver>-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` / `aarch64-…-musl` | Linux, static (any distribution) |
| `oprobe-<ver>-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` / `aarch64-…-gnu` | Linux, glibc ≥ 2.35 |
| `oprobe_<ver>-1_amd64.deb` / `_arm64.deb` | Debian, Ubuntu |
| `oprobe-<ver>-1.x86_64.rpm` / `.aarch64.rpm` | Fedora, RHEL, SUSE |
| `oprobe-desktop-<ver>-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` | Linux with the window (GTK 4.14+; `install.sh`, `.desktop` entry, icon) |
| `oprobe-<ver>-universal-apple-darwin.tar.gz` | macOS (Apple Silicon + Intel) |
| `oprobe-<ver>-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` / `x86_64-apple-darwin` | macOS single-architecture |
| `oprobe-<ver>-macos-universal.pkg` | macOS installer: `/usr/local/bin/oprobe`, man page, zsh completion |
| `oprobe-<ver>-macos-universal.dmg` | macOS app: `oprobe.app` (same binary as the `.pkg`) |
| `oprobe-<ver>-x64.msi` / `-arm64.msi` | Windows installer: `PATH`, Start menu entry, removable in *Apps* |
| `oprobe-<ver>-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` / `aarch64-…` | Windows portable |
| `oprobe.rb` / `oprobe.cask.rb` | Homebrew formula (CLI) and cask (`oprobe.app` from the `.dmg`) |
| `oprobe.json` | Scoop manifest |
| `winget-manifests.zip` | winget manifests (version, installer, locale) for the `.msi` |
| `latest.json` | machine-readable index: version, every asset's URL, size and SHA-256 |
| `install.sh` / `install.ps1` | the install scripts |
| `SHA256SUMS` | checksums of every asset |

Every build has the CLI and the terminal workbench (`oprobe top`). macOS and Windows builds also open the native
window (`oprobe gui`); the Linux `.deb`, `.rpm` and plain archives are headless (no GTK needed). Archives contain
`oprobe` (`oprobe.exe`), `README.md`, `LICENSE`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `man/`, `completions/` (bash, zsh, fish,
PowerShell, elvish), `profiles/` and `docs/`.

## Homebrew

Each release ships a formula (the CLI) and a cask (the app). Until they are in a public tap, install them from a
local tap:

```bash
brew tap-new "$USER/tools" --no-git
base=https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download
curl -fsSL "$base/oprobe.rb" -o "$(brew --repository "$USER/tools")/Formula/oprobe.rb"
curl -fsSL "$base/oprobe.cask.rb" --create-dirs -o "$(brew --repository "$USER/tools")/Casks/oprobe.rb"
brew install "$USER/tools/oprobe"            # the command line
brew install --cask "$USER/tools/oprobe"     # oprobe.app
```

Update with `brew upgrade oprobe` (`brew upgrade --cask oprobe`).

## Windows

```powershell
winget install hxddh.oprobe        # the MSI; update: winget upgrade oprobe
scoop install https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/oprobe.json
```

Maintainers submit each release to [winget-pkgs](https://github.com/microsoft/winget-pkgs) — see
[releasing.md](releasing.md#winget).

## Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora

```bash
sudo apt install ./oprobe_<ver>-1_amd64.deb
sudo dnf install ./oprobe-<ver>-1.x86_64.rpm
```

## From source

```bash
cargo install oprobe --locked
cargo install oprobe --locked --features gui
```
